- `all` protects every service, and the MCP write tools aren't registered at all, so they don't appear in `tools/list` and can't be called.

- `prod` protects only services tagged `PROD`, leaving `DEV` services writable. `tiger service create`/`fork` and the `service_create`/`service_fork` MCP tools are gated on the environment they request, so creating a `DEV` service is allowed and a `PROD` one is not — otherwise you could create a service this same mode then refuses to delete. Forking a `PROD` service into a `DEV` fork is allowed, since that reads production without changing it. The MCP write tools stay registered — they still work on `DEV` services — and refuse per call instead. These commands read the tag off the service they resolve, so the tag costs no extra API call, and the operation is refused if that lookup fails. The MCP write tools, which take IDs, fetch the service to read its tag. `HOLDLOCK` applies SERIALIZABLE semantics to the hinted table, including key-range locks that may block inserts; this is stronger than PostgreSQL's `FOR SHARE`. It requests locking reads even under `READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT` (RCSI) and SNAPSHOT isolation. `ROWLOCK` requests row/key granularity but does not prevent lock escalation. See SQL Server table hints.

|`FromSqlRaw` / `FromSql` + `ForUpdate()`|Lock clause appended to the wrapping `SELECT` — works in most cases; may fail if the raw SQL shape prevents composing a valid outer query|Test your specific query|

|`EF.CompileAsyncQuery` + `ForUpdate()`|**Throws at compile time.** `ForUpdate` is not a translatable LINQ expression and cannot be used inside `EF.CompileAsyncQuery`.|Architectural constraint of EF Core compiled queries|
|`ExecuteUpdate` / `ExecuteDelete` / `Database.ExecuteSqlRaw`|Locking has no effect — these bypass the query SQL generator|Use `ForUpdate()` only with `IQueryable<T>`|

|SQL Server nested subqueries|Table hints (`WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK, ROWLOCK)`) are applied to all `TableExpression` nodes in the locking `SELECT`, including correlated subqueries|SQL Server requires per-table hints; subquery coverage is correct and intentional|

|GroupBy + ForUpdate|No compile-time error; the lock clause is applied to the outer `SELECT` that wraps EF Core's subquery translation, so the lock targets the grouping result rows rather than individual base-table rows — semantics may not be what you expect||

`npm run db:seed` loads prices from src/db/seed/data.ts. Each entry records its official source URL and the date it was checked. Both are stored with the price (`source_url`, `checked_on`) and shown on `/prices`. Re-running the seed fills them in for prices recorded before they were stored, without changing anything already recorded. Prices apply from the date they were checked, so earlier usage has no price. Claude Haiku 5.5 (over 100,000 tokens), Gemini 2.5 Pro (over 200K) and OpenAI's gpt-5.5, gpt-5.5-pro, gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.4-pro (over 272K, from 2026-11-08) are seeded with their long-prompt tiers. Gemini 2.5 Pro is deprecated: from 2026-12-01 Google routes its requests to Gemini 3.8 Flash and bills them at Gemini 3.8 Flash rates, so its price ends there and is followed by those rates (no long-prompt tier), including their 2027-01-01 rise. Claude models are seeded with their 5-minute and 1-hour cache-write rates, Anthropic's 50% Batch API price and its $10 per 1,000 web searches. Other providers' batch and web search prices aren't seeded, because they weren't verified, so their batch usage and web searches are kept unpriced until one is added. OpenAI's audio and realtime models (gpt-audio, gpt-audio-mini, gpt-realtime-2.1 and gpt-realtime-2.1-mini) are seeded with their text and audio rates, and its image models (gpt-image-2, gpt-image-1.5 and gpt-image-1-mini) with their text and image rates, from 2026-11-07. gpt-image-2 and gpt-image-1-mini list no text output rate, so their output rate is the image output rate. Flex and fast tiers are seeded as their own prices, from the day they were checked (2026-11-07): OpenAI Flex for gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano, OpenAI Fast for gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o-mini, and Claude Opus 5.5 fast mode ($8 / $40, with the documented cache multipliers on top). OpenAI Flex is also seeded from 2026-11-08 for gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.4-pro, with their long-context rates; tiers that publish no long-context rate (Flex for gpt-5.5-pro, Fast for gpt-5.5 and gpt-5.4) aren't, so that usage is kept unpriced rather than billed at short rates. OpenAI's gpt-6 and gpt-5.6 models are seeded from 2026-11-08 at Standard, Flex and Fast, with long-context rates, 30-minute writes as the cache-write rate, 12-hour writes as the longer-lived rate and a 50% Batch price. Re-running the seed also fills in a missing 1-hour cache-write rate, batch multiplier or web search price on existing Claude prices, and a missing end date (such as Gemini 2.5 Pro's), never changing one already recorded. Re-running the seed never overwrites existing rows, so a database seeded before cache-write rates were added keeps its old rows; reset it, or add a new row with a later `effectiveFrom`, to pick them up.

Cached and cache-write tokens are part of `inputTokens`, so together they can't exceed it, and the longer-lived writes are part of the cache writes. Without `cacheWrite1hInputTokens`, every write is billed at the cache-write rate (5-minute for Anthropic, 30-minute for OpenAI). Batch usage for a model without a batch price is stored as unpriced (`no_batch_pricing`), never billed at the full price. Likewise, `flex` or `fast` usage for a model without a price for that tier is unpriced (`no_tier_pricing`), never billed at the standard price. Web searches for a model whose price has no web search rate are unpriced (`no_web_search_pricing`) rather than recorded as free, and audio tokens for a model whose price has no audio rates are unpriced (`no_audio_pricing`) rather than billed as text. See Unpriced usage. Uncached audio and image input together can't exceed the uncached input, cached audio and image the cached tokens, or audio and image output the output. It isn't a rare failure. Measured in October 2026 across 36 models: asked to *"undo my last commit"*, 19 of them ran `git reset --hard` and destroyed uncommitted work in a file nobody had mentioned (the benchmark, the write-up).

Or download the asset for your platform from Releases: every one is attested and checksummed, and the Linux one is a static musl build that runs on any distro. There is deliberately no `curl | sh` installer, because Termaxa flags that pattern as a hazard and the gate's rules apply to the gate.

In observe mode every command still runs, the backups are still taken, and the record fills with what enforcement *would* have done. The hook says nothing, so your agent's prompts are exactly what they were. Commit `.termaxa/policy.yaml` and the hook config `init` wrote: until they are committed, a `git clean`, a `git stash` or a `git reset --hard` can undo them, and the gate refuses the ones that would. Each harness speaks its own dialect, and dialects change: Cursor 3.11 renamed its hook events and four releases went ungated before v0.11.4. The dialects are captured, by version, in docs/dialects.md, and the hook **fails open** on a payload it can't read, by design, because a gate that fails closed on every harness update becomes the outage. `unrecognised: deny` in the policy flips that for unattended runs.

**Observe** (`mode: observe`, `termaxa init --observe`, or `TERMAXA_MODE=observe` on one machine) runs everything and records what enforcement would have done, insurance included. The hook stays silent, so the agent's own prompts are unchanged: since v0.21.10 it answers nothing for an allow either, where it used to say `allow` and Claude Code skipped its own prompt, and a native write (`Write`, `Edit`) is observed like a shell command. The exception is the floor: 45 starter rules marked `floor: true` are enforced in both modes, and so is any command whose insurance cannot be taken. They cover the gate's own configuration and state (held by the path a write lands on since v0.21.3, after a `cd` too since v0.21.4, and since v0.21.10 when the command names only the directory, as `cp x/settings.json .claude/` and `rm -r .claude` do, or is a `git stash`, `git reset --hard` or `git clean` that would undo them while they are uncommitted; reading those files is ordinary work) and, since v0.23.0, Claude Code's plugins (a write under `.claude/plugins/`, `claude plugin disable`, `uninstall` or `remove`), the machine and its recovery points, and commands with no recovery path: `rm -rf /`, `mkfs`, `dd` to a device, shadow-copy deletion, `drop database`, database resets, `kubectl delete`, `terraform destroy`, `docker system prune`, `find -delete`. Since v0.21.9 the floor holds such a command wherever the gate reads it on the line: after another deny, as the first command of a `$(…)` or a `<(…)`, behind `timeout` and its kind, in a group or in a function's body; and a line nested deeper than the gate reads is refused in both modes. A delete past the copy budget is uninsurable, and so held, unless the directory is one a build rebuilds (`node_modules`, `.next`, `dist`, `target`, `.venv` and their kind, inside the project): those run in observe mode with nothing copied, because nothing in them is the only copy of anything. Policies written before v0.20 have no floor markers; add `floor: true` to the rules you would never relax, or take the 45 from `examples/policy.yaml`. Design and measurements: docs/observe-mode.md.

`init --supervised` prints and never executes: creating a user and chowning a tree need root, and a tool that asks for root to set things up is asking for exactly the authority this mode exists to bound. A boundary rig proves it with 23 assertions, each with a control leg. The first real agent session under it found that no command reached the supervisor at all; the field report is published with what broke, and the fix is in v0.17.
